S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, injury, evacuation, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a fuller incident report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk, and provide practical safety instructions and subsequent updates.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, injury, evacuation, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a fuller incident report within 10 business days. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk, and provide practical safety instructions and subsequent updates. Reports must include known incident counts and be corrected promptly if material information changes.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: The maximum permitted failure rate is 7% of tested units per model. Manufacturers must provide complete model-specific test results, including failure rates, to the regulator and to customers considering or using that model. Results may be provided directly to those customers and need not be posted publicly.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter. The maximum permitted failure rate is 7% of tested units per model. Manufacturers must provide complete model-specific test results, including failure rates, to the regulator and to customers considering or using that model. Results may be provided directly to those customers and need not be posted publicly. If a model exceeds the limit, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers within 10 business days, provide practical safety instructions, and submit a corrective-action plan; the regulator may require retesting or restrict sales based on the results and safety evidence.

parameters.quote: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support this function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved protective measure, within 6 years after adoption.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support this function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved protective measure, within 6 years after adoption.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support this function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved protective measure, within 6 years after adoption. Customers must receive clear instructions on how to use the shut-off function and its limitations.

parameters.quote: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment, and its maintenance requirements must be disclosed to customers.

parameters.quote: A mandatory safety response is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling 12-month period. The manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and implement a recall or other regulator-approved remedy. Exceeding the threshold requires this safety response but does not by itself require an automatic market ban; the regulator may require a recall based on other evidence of an imminent safety risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A mandatory safety response is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling 12-month period. The manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and implement a recall or other regulator-approved remedy. Exceeding the threshold requires this safety response but does not by itself require an automatic market ban; the regulator may require a recall based on other evidence of an imminent safety risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase and at installation, customers must receive clear safety instructions, emergency contact details, and information on safety notices or required precautions for their model. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material safety risks and provide interim protective steps. A mandatory safety response is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling 12-month period. The rate must use the model’s installed-unit population and count distinct incidents; manufacturers must promptly correct material reporting errors. The manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and implement a recall or other regulator-approved remedy. Exceeding the threshold requires this safety response but does not by itself require an automatic market ban; the regulator may require a recall based on other evidence of an imminent safety risk.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: For a complete evidence base, Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate at 55 °C and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. Those figures do not support treating a 5% limit as an established evidence-based cutoff. I propose a 7% limit with confidential per-model results to regulators, prompt corrective action for exceedances, and customer notices describing material risks and precautions without publishing individual failure rates.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 sets a 7% permanent failure cap with no sales stop and numeric per-model results provided to customers and the regulator but not published, which is the central compromise. S3 gives a 6-year retrofit window (Northwind's red line) and S4 sets suppression at 36 months (Halcyon's red line), both within acceptable ranges. S5 keeps an 8-per-100k trigger but replaces mandatory recall with an open-ended 'recall or other regulator-approved remedy', which favours Halcyon's Ember 8 and is the weakest section.
